qualifications.am-u02-ssm-2026-machado-ai-governance-co: The speech addresses risks to individual banks from a supervisory perspective; its one mention of systemic scale concerns AI usage, not provider dependence. Recorded as context after a second check by a model of another family; it does not quantify concentration or state that a provider failure has occurred. No views disclaimer was found on the page.
qualifications.am-u05-dn-2019-text-ml-bankruptcy: Quoted from the Danish summary on the landing page; the PDF of the Analysis (No. 3, read 2026-11-04, the same file as a second check by a model of another family read) states the same finding in its summary (“Det øger nøjagtigheden af de beregnede konkurssandsynligheder”). The PDF credits Anna Kirstine Hvid and Pia Mølgaard, Quantitative Risk Analysts, Financial Stability (p. 7), and prints no statement that the views are theirs alone: the voice is the Nationalbank’s analytical series, with staff credits, not a claim that the text is anonymous. The modelling serves the Nationalbank’s financial-stability analysis; the underlying working paper of November 2018 is a separate document, not recorded.
qualifications.am-u09-fsb-2017-ai-ml: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The June 2017 FSB report uses the word “SupTech” only in its glossary, without reference to AI. This November 2017 report uses the term together with AI. The earliest located use of the name is the June 2017 FSB report.
qualifications.am-u09-bcbs-2018-sound-practices-fintech: Not earliest located; the report itself cites earlier texts. It describes supervisors’ involvement with suptech as nascent and names lack of transparency of AI as a barrier.
qualifications.am-u12-imf-2021-dp-ai-finance-context: A staff paper attributed to its authors. Read with the rule that a call for guidance or adaptation in specific areas does not, alone, contest broad coverage: it calls for standards and guidance in specific areas, and states no view on whether existing frameworks broadly cover AI.
qualifications.am-u12-fsi-2024-insights-63: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer; the same summary says that guidance may be needed in specific areas, which is recorded on J12 as context.
qualifications.am-u12-fsi-2024-insights-63-context: Recorded as context after a check by a model of another family: further guidance and the oversight of providers coexist with broad coverage. The text also articulates J12; the paper says authorities ‘may need to examine existing regulations and, if needed, issue clarifications, revisions or even new regulations’ in listed areas.
qualifications.am-u12-rbi-2025-free-ai-report-context: A second check by a model of another family (2026-11-04) read it this way, and the reading was agreed: the dedicated institutional framework of paragraph 4.4.33 is an institution for risk assessment, coordination and standard-setting, not a separate regulatory regime; with the incremental additions and conditional amendments it does not contest broad coverage. The report also recommends guiding regulated entities on how existing regulations apply to AI. The committee’s text, not stated by the RBI to be its policy.
qualifications.am-u12-boe-2026-breeden-agents-of-change: Read with the rule that a call for guidance or adaptation in specific areas does not, alone, contest broad coverage: a question and a possible adaptation for autonomous agents, not a contest of broad coverage. She does not propose specific AI-specific rules. Compare her speech of 31 October 2024, also recorded on J12. A second check by a model of another family reads the passage as a qualified, prospective contest of continuing sufficiency for autonomous agents (frameworks not built for them; a human in the loop unlikely to be realistic), while noting that the distinction drawn here is reasonable and that the next sentence allows adapted governance frameworks. The record keeps that uncertainty.
qualifications.am-u12-fsb-2026-ai-sound-practices-conte: Recorded as context after a check by a model of another family. The report also notes that some standard-setting bodies have issued AI-specific guidance and that some risks of agentic AI are newer; the record does not show that no AI-specific rules exist or are needed.
qualifications.am-event-fsb-2017-ai-ml-monitoring: States work in progress; the record does not show when the monitoring began or what it produced beyond the annex. The text states the work as under way at its date; it is recorded as a dated statement of status, never as a completed event. No start or completion date is stated.
qualifications.am-event-pbc-2022-ai-algorithm-evaluatio: The reply does not give the standard’s number or issue date; the standard code JR/T 0221-2021 and the date 2021-03-26 appear in the PBoC financial-standards disclosure system, whose record page could not be read when the record was prepared (script-rendered), so neither is taken as evidenced here. English rendering is a paraphrase.
qualifications.am-event-fsb-2024-ai-report-update: An official’s statement in a speech; the speech’s disclaimer states that the views are not necessarily those of the FSB or its members. The text states the update as under way at its date; it is recorded as a dated statement of status, never as a completed event or a launch. No start or completion date is stated. The FSB report of 14 November 2024 is recorded separately as a document. A later paragraph calls the work analytical, with no policy options then.
qualifications.am-event-rb-2025-ai-policy: The decision states adoption and an entry-into-force date; the record does not show how the policy has been applied. Recorded as a dated statement of status.
qualifications.am-event-fsb-2026-frontier-ai-cyber-work: The record states work under exploration, not its outcome. The text states the work as under way at its date; it is recorded as a dated statement of status, never as a completed event. No start or completion date is stated.
qualifications.am-event-ecb-2024-ai-action-plan: The plan is described in a speech; this record does not show that the plan was published or what it contains.

object.value: restarting operations at the Crane Clean Energy Center in 2027 (stated target)

row.statement: Constellation stated in its second-quarter results release of 6 August 2026 that the NRC’s approval of a fuel licence amendment request for the Crane Clean Energy Center was a major milestone moving it closer to restarting operations in 2027.

time.note: Date of the release (dateline 6 August 2026); the target year is Constellation’s.

row.qualification: Constellation’s stated target, dated by its release: not an NRC authorisation of a restart and not evidence that the plant has restarted or will. The NRC’s facility page lists the approvals a restart would need. Constellation’s announcement of September 2024 gave a 2028 online date.

entries.old: Rests on the NRC's own record: its facility page and its Federal Register notice of the amendment. The amendment allows receipt and possession of new fuel and sealed neutron sources; the facility page lists the approvals a restart would need separately, and the record does not say the plant may restart or operate. The amendment document itself (ADAMS ML26135A004) was refused at retrieval. Constellation's statement of 6 August 2026, attributed to it as context, calls the step the approval of a fuel licence amendment request and gives 2027 as its target for restarting operations; the target is Constellation's, not the NRC's, and is not recorded as a stated date of this record.

row.statement: The abstract of Periola and Kolawole’s article on space-based data centres (2019) states that relying on further terrestrial data centres becomes problematic in densely populated regions, which leads to exploring space as a place to host them.
